title: Pressure-cooker pho-style broth
subtitle: A warming, aromatic beef broth in 45 minutes
excerpt: A deeply aromatic Vietnamese-inspired broth with beef, star anise, cinnamon, and ginger cooked under pressure. Traditional pho takes 6 to 8 hours; this version produces a truly flavoured result in under an hour.
sourceNotes: Pho bò (beef pho) originated in northern Vietnam in the early 20th century, likely influenced by French and Chinese culinary traditions. The broth is traditionally simmered for 6 to 8 hours with charred aromatics. The pressure-cooker version is a widely used adaptation that compresses the technique.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the broth alone (strained, without toppings) for up to 4 months. Add fresh toppings when reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The broth is better the next day. Strain and refrigerate for up to 4 days.

content.text: A pho-style broth from the pressure cooker is a home adaptation rather than a traditional recipe, real pho takes the better part of a day to make. This version captures the essential character: a clear, deeply beefy broth scented with star anise, cinnamon, and charred ginger, with the toppings assembled in the bowl. It takes about 45 minutes at high pressure and is truly good.

Charring the ginger and onion before adding them to the pot is important, this is what gives the broth its characteristic sweet smokiness. Hold each piece directly over a gas flame with tongs, or place under a very hot grill until charred and fragrant.

Serve with thinly sliced beef stirred into the hot broth (it cooks in the heat of the bowl), fresh herbs, bean sprouts, lime, and chilli. The toppings are not optional, they are how the dish is eaten.

items.prepNote: halved, charred over flame or under grill
sliced, charred over flame or under grill
very thinly sliced, to serve raw in the bowl

content.text: Char the halved onion and ginger directly over a gas flame until darkened on the surface, or place under a very hot grill for 8 to 10 minutes turning once. This step gives the broth its characteristic smoky-sweet character.

Put the oxtail, charred onion and ginger, star anise, cinnamon, garlic, soy sauce, and {{stock-beef}} of beef stock in the pressure cooker. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 45 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 15 minutes.

Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discard the solids. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and soy sauce. Bring to a simmer. Ladle into warm bowls over a handful of rice noodles (cooked separately according to packet instructions). Lay thin slices of raw beef across the top, the hot broth cooks them in the bowl. Serve with lime wedges, fresh herbs, and chilli.

rows.cause: The oxtail released fat and collagen during pressure cooking.
rows.fix: This does not affect flavour. For a clearer broth, chill overnight, lift off the solidified fat, and reheat.

rows.cause: The star anise cooked for too long or the quantity was too high.
rows.fix: Use 2 rather than 3 stars next time. Strain the broth immediately and taste, if still too strong, dilute with more stock.

content.text: Pho is a bowl that rewards attention, a clear, aromatic broth assembled at the table with fresh herbs, lime, and thinly sliced meat that cooks in the heat of the serving. The pressure-cooker home adaptation is not identical to the real thing, but it captures enough of the character to be worth making regularly. It is winter comfort food with a different register from European broth-based soups.
